newsitem.title: JAPAN: Will US-Japan port row follow trade spat script?.
newsitem.headline: Will US-Japan port row follow trade spat script?.

text.p: Fans of U.S.-Japan trade friction dramas just might see a surprise ending to a fresh feud over shipping if key actors refuse to read from the time-honoured script of sanction threats and last-ditch deals.

Past trade disputes, including a bitter row over automotive trade two years ago, have often followed a pattern in which negotiators go to the brink but avert threatened U.S. sanctions with an eleventh-hour deal forged by veteran trade negotiators.
Will this spring see a re-run of the typical drama?

The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) said on Wednesday that it would slap $100,000 surcharges on Japanese vessels calling at U.S. ports in retaliation for what it termed "unfavourable restrictive practices. The commission added that the surcharges would become effective on April 14.
On Thursday, Japan said it was trying to fix the problem and urged the United States to withdraw its sanctions threat.

Tokyo also warned the row could hurt bilateral ties and said implementing the sanctions might violate world trade rules and a U.S.-Japan treaty. Japanese ship owners bemoaned the sanctions threat and said they would be innocent victims.
A Japanese official, meanwhile, said the two sides would meet, possibly next week, to discuss the dispute.
Thus far, the plot sounds familiar.
Washington, irritated at a lack of progress, moves closer to sanctions. Japan protests but expresses willingness to talk, and the clock starts ticking.
Thus it was in 1995, when the two nations went to the brink in a bitter battle over automotive trade, only to forge a deal at the last minute to avert threatened U.S. sanctions.
A Japanese government official said, however, that history might not repeat itself.

For one thing, two key players -- the FMC and the Japan Harbour Transportation Association (JHTA), which is made up of port cargo-handling firms and mediates between unions and shipping companies -- will not be at the negotiating table when transport officials and diplomats from the two sides meet.

At the heart of the dispute are U.S. charges that the JHTA has put in place costly and discriminatory practices through a "prior consultation" system of negotiations and pre-approvals involving carriers, JHTA and waterfront unions.
Washington also says Japan's licensing requirements for terminal operators and stevedoring firms discriminate against foreign firms.
"This time the story might be more difficult. Two main players are not taking part in the talks," the Japanese official said.

Getting the JHTA to agree to changes proposed by foreign shipowners -- Europe has also complained about Japan's port practices -- could be tough given the strength and political clout of the waterfront labour unions, the official added.

Foreign shipowners have long been frustrated by Japan's harbour practices, which Japanese film makers have portrayed as controlled by "yakuza," or gangsters. "They are very strong labour unions, including politically," the official said.

The FMC, meanwhile, might prove less susceptible to the diplomatic and political considerations some trade experts say convinced U.S. trade officials to forge deals in the past, a U.S. source suggested.
"They are very independent and value that independence," the source said. "They don't necessarily play the same political games."
A U.S. official, however, flatly dismissed the notion that the FMC's independence would affect the outcome of the row and told Reuters he was optimistic that sanctions would be averted.
